analysis.one_liner: Protects roughly 20 million acres of Northern Rockies federal land as wilderness and bans logging, mining, and drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 153 cosponsors but never received a hearing markup or floor vote in the House Resources Committee, and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have permanently protected about 15 million acres of federal land in Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming as wilderness, plus millions more as connecting wildlife corridors where logging, mining, oil and gas drilling, and new road-building would be barred [S2, S3]. It would also have created a new Hells Canyon national preserve, added wild and scenic rivers, set up a wildland restoration corps to repair damaged forests, and guaranteed Native American tribes traditional and religious access to the protected lands [S2, S3]. It was introduced by Rep. Christopher Shays (R-CT) and gathered 153 cosponsors, but never left committee [S4, S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, hikers, anglers, hunters on foot, scientists, and anyone who values clean water and intact forests would have gained permanent access to vast wild landscapes. Rural communities could have gained jobs in ecosystem restoration through the new Wildland Recovery Corps. Tribes, notably the Blackfeet, would have gained formal protection of religious and treaty lands, and the bill explicitly guaranteed Native Americans traditional cultural and religious access to the protected areas [S3]. Taxpayers would also have gained by ending federal logging programs that, as the bill's own findings state, return less to the Treasury than the land is worth undeveloped [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hikers, anglers, tribes, and downstream water users

how_it_helps.text: The bill designates six large ecosystems in the Northern Rockies as wilderness, permanently barring road construction, logging, mining, and oil and gas development on those lands [S2, S3].

It links the protected ecosystems with biological connecting corridors of about 8.4 million acres, where timber harvesting, mining, oil and gas development, and new roads are prohibited, to keep wildlife populations connected between core habitats [S3].
It reserves federal water rights with the date of enactment as priority for each wilderness area, protecting stream flows for fish and downstream users [S3].

It establishes the Blackfeet Wilderness over the Badger-Two Medicine area, recognizes Blackfeet treaty rights, and guarantees Native Americans nonexclusive access to designated areas for traditional cultural and religious purposes [S3].

It creates a National Wildland Restoration and Recovery System and a Wildland Recovery Corps to repair forest lands damaged by logging and road building, a potential source of restoration jobs in rural communities [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies, hardrock mining companies, and oil and gas developers would lose access to millions of acres of federal land now open to them, and some motorized recreation users would lose areas to ride. Rural counties whose economies and federal road payments have historically depended on national forest logging would bear the hardest transition. The bill's own findings argue that the land left undeveloped is worth more to the nation than the timber revenue it could return, and note that taxpayers currently fund the development [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation is the strictest form of federal land protection: it bars logging, mining, drilling, new roads, and generally motorized travel, so the bill takes land off the table permanently rather than managing trade-offs case by case [S2, S3].

Restricting timber harvest and mining would cut jobs and local government revenue in some rural Northern Rockies communities that have depended on those activities on federal land; the bill's restoration corps could not fully offset that loss, and the bill leaves the transition unaddressed [S3].

The designations were written from Washington, DC, by a sponsor from Connecticut and cosponsors mostly from outside the region, over the objections that the region's congressional delegation and local users were largely not behind this version of the bill, an honest criticism its supporters had to answer [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The conservation gains are enormous and permanent, and the bill was drafted with real care: it exempts named public highways, exempts all private land, allows willing-seller land trades, and protects treaty rights [S3]. The costs fall on a small set of extractive industries and on some rural communities dependent on federal logging, a cost the bill acknowledges but only partially offsets through restoration work. The main honest objection is not that the protection is worthless but that it is total, and that a bill of this scale would ideally carry a serious economic transition plan for timber-dependent counties. On balance, the bill's own finding that the land is worth more undeveloped than harvested, with taxpayer-subsidized development, makes a strong case that ordinary people come out ahead [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee and to two of its subcommittees on February 15, 2001, and that is where the paper trail ends: no hearing, no markup, no vote ever came, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Shays (R-CT) introduced the bill on February 6, 2001, with 36 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Resources [S1, S3, S5].

On February 15, 2001, it was referred to the subcommittees on National Parks, Recreation and Public Lands and on Forests and Forest Health, with executive comment requested from the Agriculture and Interior Departments [S5].
The bill accumulated 153 cosponsors: 141 of 208 House Democrats, 11 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's 1 Independent [S4].

No further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the 107th Congress: the bill never received a hearing, a subcommittee or full committee vote, or a floor vote, and died with the Congress on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never got a vote, the timber, mining, and oil and gas companies that would have lost access to these public lands are better off, as are the managers of the status quo: federal forests remain open to logging, mining, drilling, and road building under the preexisting rules, and none of the protected acreage or restoration funding was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber, mining, and drilling interests kept the land open

sides.party_line_note: The bill was formally bipartisan, sponsored by a Connecticut Republican, but its support was overwhelmingly Democratic: 141 of 208 House Democrats cosponsored versus only 11 of 223 House Republicans, and the committee chaired by a Republican that held it never acted.

industries.note: The bill prohibits timber harvesting across the wilderness areas and connecting corridors, taking millions of acres of federal forest off the timber supply permanently. Because federal logging programs are heavily subsidized by taxpayers, this loss to the industry was a gain to the public, which is why the industry's interest ran against the public's in this bill [S3].

The bill bars mining across the wilderness areas and corridors, including a withdrawal of the Badger-Two Medicine area from the mining and mineral leasing laws. The public gains undeveloped land and water quality; the industry loses access it currently holds [S3].

Oil and gas exploration and development is prohibited in the wilderness areas and connecting corridors, removing those federal lands from leasing. What the industry would have gained by drilling is land the public would have permanently lost [S3].

Wilderness and corridor management require road densities approaching zero, ending most motorized access in the designated areas. Some backcountry users lose access, while non-motorized users gain it; this is a redistribution within the public rather than a transfer to a concentrated interest [S3].

Counties that historically drew revenue and jobs from federal logging would face a difficult transition, partially offset by restoration jobs under the new Wildland Recovery Corps. Their interest in continued logging ran against the conservation interest of the broader public [S3].

The bill creates the Blackfeet Wilderness over the Badger-Two Medicine area, recognizes Blackfeet treaty rights, and guarantees Native Americans traditional and religious access to the protected areas. This is a direct public and tribal gain with no offsetting industry cost [S3].
